title: Functions & Modules
goal: You will learn to make your own functions, understand parameters, default/keyword args, *args/**kwargs, return, scope, lambda, map/filter and recursion, and split your code into clean files by importing modules.

lessons.title: What is a function — def and parameters
blocks: **Function** = a **reusable block** of code. Write it once, give it a name, and call it by name whenever you need it. No need to repeat code.
A tea machine: press the button (function call), the process inside (body) runs, and tea comes out (result). You don't have to build the machine again every time.
Real use: in an ERP, build "calculate tax" once, then call it in 100 places. If you find a mistake, fix it in just one place.

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello {name}! Welcome to GEEP")

greet("Anna")
greet("Rohan")
greet("Deepak")

Hello Anna! Welcome to GEEP
Hello Rohan! Welcome to GEEP
Hello Deepak! Welcome to GEEP
**Defining** and **calling** are two different things. `def` only writes the recipe; nothing runs until you call it.
**Parameter** vs **argument**: the name you write in the brackets when making the function (`name`) is the parameter. The real value you send when calling (`"Anna"`) is the argument.

def cable_cost(meters, rate):
    print(f"{meters} m x Rs {rate} = Rs {meters * rate}")

cable_cost(100, 45)
cable_cost(250, 38)
Look carefully: arguments go by **order**. The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second.
Common mistake: calling a function before defining it gives `NameError`. Python reads from top to bottom, so `def` must come first.
Common mistake: sending too few or too many arguments. If you write `cable_cost(100)` you get `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'rate'`.
**Docstring** = a small note in triple quotes at the start of a function: what the function does. In professional code every function has a docstring.

def area(length, width):
    """Rectangle ka area return karta hai."""
    return length * width

print(area.__doc__)
Rectangle ka area return karta hai.
Name a function like a **verb** that tells its job: `calculate_tax`, `clean_text`, `load_data`. And one function = one job.

lessons.title: return vs print — getting a value back
blocks: `print` = **shown** on the screen, that's it. `return` = value **handed back to you**, now you can use it further.

def add_print(a, b):
    print(a + b)

def add_return(a, b):
    return a + b

x = add_print(2, 3)
print("x =", x)
y = add_return(2, 3)
print("y =", y)
print("y * 10 =", y * 10)
Look carefully: `add_print` showed 5, but `x` got **None**. A function without `return` quietly returns `None`.
The shopkeeper **shows** you the bill (print) vs **hands** you the bill (return). Only if it is in your hand can you submit it at the office later.
In real projects 99% of functions `return`. `predictions = model.predict(data)` — `predict` returns, it doesn't print, so the result can be used further.

def calculate_tax(salary, tax_percent=10):
    tax = salary * tax_percent / 100
    net = salary - tax
    return net

s1 = calculate_tax(50000)
s2 = calculate_tax(80000, 20)
print(f"50K salary, 10% tax: {s1}")
print(f"80K salary, 20% tax: {s2}")
Common mistake: writing `return net` but never creating a variable called `net` (you wrote `salary = salary - tax`). Result: `NameError`. Return the variable you actually created.
After `return` the function **stops right away**. The lines below don't run. This is called an **early return**.
**Returning multiple values:** use commas. Python packs them into one **tuple**, and you can open them into separate boxes (**unpacking**).

def cable_report(length, defects):
    quality = "PASS" if defects == 0 else "FAIL"
    cost = length * 50
    return quality, cost

q, c = cable_report(100, 0)
print(f"Quality: {q}, Cost: {c}")
print(cable_report(200, 3))
You will see this everywhere in ML: `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(...)` — one function, four values back.

lessons.title: Default, keyword, *args and **kwargs
blocks: **Default parameter:** if no value is given, a preset value is used. GST is mostly 18%, so set the default to 18.

def total(rate, meters, gst=18):
    amount = rate * meters
    return amount + amount * gst / 100

print(total(100, 10))
print(total(100, 10, 5))
Parameters with defaults always go **at the end**. Writing `def f(gst=18, rate):` gives a SyntaxError.
**Keyword arguments:** give values by name when calling. Then order doesn't matter, and the code is easier to read.

def total(rate, meters, gst=18):
    amount = rate * meters
    return amount + amount * gst / 100

print(total(meters=10, rate=100))
print(total(100, 10, gst=12))
Keyword arguments are everywhere in ML libraries: `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=5, random_state=42)`. The names tell you which value is for what.
`*args` = send as many positional values as you like, they all land in one **tuple**.
`**kwargs` = send as many **named** values as you like, they all land in one **dictionary** (dict in detail in Stage 4).

name = Akash
city = Bhiwadi
role = developer
Remember: **one star = tuple, two stars = dict.** The names `args`/`kwargs` are just a convention; the real work is done by `*` and `**`.
When all are used together the order is fixed: normal → `*args` → default/keyword-only → `**kwargs`.
Common mistake (IQ favourite): **mutable default**. `def add_item(item, lst=[]):` — this list is created only **once** and the same old list is used in every call.

def add_item(item, lst=[]):
    lst.append(item)
    return lst

print(add_item("a"))
print(add_item("b"))

def add_item_safe(item, lst=None):
    if lst is None:
        lst = []
    lst.append(item)
    return lst

print(add_item_safe("a"))
print(add_item_safe("b"))
Fix: set the default to `None` and create a new list inside. Never put `[]` or `{}` as a default.

lessons.title: Scope — how far a variable can be seen
blocks: **Scope** = the area where a variable can be seen and used. A variable made inside a function is **local**: alive only inside, and when the function ends, it ends too.
Rooms in a house: something kept inside a room (local) is found only in that room. Something kept in the courtyard (global) can be seen from every room.

andar: 10
bahar: NameError -> name 'x' is not defined
(`try/except` is a way to catch errors, in detail in Stage 5. Here it is just to show the error.)
A **global** variable (made at the top level of the file) can be **read** inside a function:

rate = 45

def cost(meters):
    return meters * rate

print(cost(10))
But if you **assign a value** to the same name inside the function, Python creates a **new local** variable. The outside one does not change.

count = 0

def bump():
    count = 99
    print("andar:", count)

bump()
print("bahar:", count)
If you really want to change the outside one, use the `global` keyword:

count = 0

def bump():
    global count
    count += 1

bump()
bump()
print(count)

Use `global` as little as possible. When every function quietly changes globals, bugs become hard to find. Better way: **pass the value in as a parameter, get it back with return**: `count = bump(count)`.
Python's order for finding a name: **LEGB** — Local, Enclosing (the outer function), Global, Built-in (like `print`, `len`).

blocks.title: LEGB: where to find a name

blocks: Common mistake: using a built-in name for a variable, like `sum = 10` or `list = [1, 2]`. Then `sum([1, 2])` gives an error, because the global `sum` hides the built-in.

lessons.title: lambda, map, filter and recursion
blocks: **lambda** = a small one-line function without a name. Format: `lambda inputs: expression`. No need to write `return`, the value of the expression comes back on its own.

square = lambda x: x * x
print(square(4))

def square2(x):
    return x * x
print(square2(4))
The real use of lambda: giving a small job to another function, like the key for **sorting**.

leads = [("Rahul", 500), ("Neha", 900), ("Amit", 300)]
print(sorted(leads, key=lambda l: l[1]))
print(max(leads, key=lambda l: l[1]))
`key=lambda l: l[1]` means "sort by looking at index 1 (amount) of each item".
**map** = apply a function to every item. **filter** = keep only the items for which the function gives True. You must wrap both in `list()` to see the result.

prices = [100, 250, 80, 400]
with_gst = list(map(lambda p: round(p * 1.18, 2), prices))
print(with_gst)
costly = list(filter(lambda p: p > 150, prices))
print(costly)
Many people prefer **list comprehension** over map/filter: `[p * 1.18 for p in prices]`. That is in Stage 4. For an IQ you should know both.
**Recursion** = a function that **calls itself**. Every recursion needs two things: a **base case** (when to stop) and a **smaller problem** (each call makes the problem smaller).
Going down stairs: "go down one step, then go down the rest of the steps". When you reach the floor (base case), stop.
Each call is placed on top of a **stack** (a pile of plates). As soon as the base case is reached, answers return back down: 1, 2, 6, 24.
Common mistake: if you forget the base case, the function keeps calling itself and you get `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded` (default limit is about 1000).

def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("GO!")
        return
    print(n, end=" ")
    countdown(n - 1)

countdown(3)
Recursion is natural for trees, folders and nested data. But for simple counting a loop is faster and safer.

lessons.title: Modules, import and __name__ == "__main__"
blocks: **Module** = a `.py` file that has functions and variables. With **import** you use code from another file in your file. Python comes with many free modules (the **standard library**).
Toolbox: you don't need to make every tool yourself. `import math` = you opened the maths box.

import math
print(math.sqrt(16))
print(math.pi)
print(math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(4.8))

from math import sqrt, pi
print(sqrt(25))

import statistics as st
print(st.mean([2, 4, 6]))
`import numpy as np`, `import pandas as pd` — this **alias** (short name) is the standard across the whole ML world. You will write it daily in Stage 8.
Common mistake: `from module import *` — all names come in at once and can clash with your variables. Avoid it.
Set a **seed** with the `random` module and you get the same "random" numbers every time. In ML this is the same idea used to repeat results (`random_state=42`).

import random
random.seed(42)
print(random.randint(1, 100), random.randint(1, 100))
random.seed(42)
print(random.randint(1, 100), random.randint(1, 100))
**Making your own module**: create a file `cable_utils.py` and write functions in it. Then import it in another file.
Running `python cable_utils.py` prints `Test: 450`. But running `python main.py` gives only `4500` — the test line will **not** run.
Why? Every file has a special variable `__name__`. If you **run the file directly**, `__name__` = `"__main__"`. If the file is **imported**, `__name__` = the file's name (`"cable_utils"`).
Rule: put every script's "run" code inside `if __name__ == "__main__":`. Then the file can be both a **module** and a **script**. FastAPI, training scripts all use this pattern.
**pip** installs outside packages: `pip install numpy`. Then `import numpy` will work. The standard library doesn't need installing.

teach.say: A function is a reusable box of code. Make it once with def, then call it by name as many times as you like.
The name written in the brackets is the parameter. The value you send when calling is the argument.
print only shows, return gives the value back. If there is no return, the function gives None.
With commas you can return many values. They come in a tuple, and we open them into separate boxes.
A default value makes a parameter optional, and with a keyword argument you send the value with its name, so no worry about order.
One star args collects all extra values into a tuple, two star kwargs collects named values into a dict.
A variable made inside a function is local, it isn't visible outside. The order for finding a name is LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
lambda is a one-line function without a name. It is most useful as a sorting key, and in map and filter.
In recursion a function calls itself. A base case is a must, otherwise RecursionError. Each call goes up on the stack and the answer comes back down.
A module is just a py file. Use it with import. And the code inside if name equals main runs only when the file is run directly, not on import. Now go practice!

practice.q:
Write a function `mean_std(nums)` that returns both the **mean** and the **standard deviation** (population) of the numbers. Don't use a library, work it out yourself with loops. Output:
Mean: 5.0
Std: 2.0
practice.starter:
def mean_std(nums):
    # TODO: mean = total / count
    # TODO: add (x - mean) ** 2 for every number, divide by count, then ** 0.5
    pass

m, s = mean_std([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(f"Mean: {m}")
print(f"Std: {s}")
practice.hint: Two loops: first the mean from the total, then the total of squared differences. `return mean, std` gives both back.
practice.solution:
def mean_std(nums):
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
    mean = total / len(nums)
    sq = 0
    for x in nums:
        sq += (x - mean) ** 2
    std = (sq / len(nums)) ** 0.5
    return mean, std

m, s = mean_std([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(f"Mean: {m}")
print(f"Std: {s}")

practice.q:
**Min-max scaling** (common ML preprocessing): write a function `scale(x, lo, hi)` that returns `(x - lo) / (hi - lo)`. Then scale all values with `map` + `lambda`, and use `filter` to count how many are 0.5 or more. Output:
[0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
High values: 3
practice.starter:
def scale(x, lo, hi):
    # TODO: return the formula
    pass

values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
lo, hi = min(values), max(values)
# TODO: scaled = list(map(lambda ..., values))
# TODO: high = list(filter(lambda ..., scaled))
# TODO: print both
practice.hint: `map(lambda v: scale(v, lo, hi), values)`. In the filter lambda the condition is `v >= 0.5`.
practice.solution:
def scale(x, lo, hi):
    return (x - lo) / (hi - lo)

values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
lo, hi = min(values), max(values)
scaled = list(map(lambda v: scale(v, lo, hi), values))
print(scaled)
high = list(filter(lambda v: v >= 0.5, scaled))
print(f"High values: {len(high)}")

quiz.q: What does a function without `return` return?
quiz.why: A function without return automatically returns `None`.

quiz.q: If `def total(rate, meters, gst=18)`, what is gst in `total(100, 10)`?
quiz.why: gst was not given, so the default value 18 was used.

quiz.q: If `def f(*args): return args`, what does `f(1, 2, 3)` give?
quiz.why: *args packs all extra positional values into one tuple.

quiz.q: What type do the values inside `**kwargs` come in?
quiz.why: Named values are key-value pairs, so a dict is made.

quiz.q: What is the result of `(lambda x: x * 2)(5)`?
quiz.why: lambda got 5, and the expression 5 * 2 = 10 came back.

quiz.q: Inside a function you made `x = 10`. What happens on `print(x)` outside (no x outside)?
quiz.why: x is local, it exists only inside the function.

quiz.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
quiz.why: The function keeps calling itself until the recursion limit (~1000) is crossed, then RecursionError.

quiz.q: When does the code inside `if __name__ == "__main__":` run?
o: When the file is run directly
quiz.why: When run directly `__name__` is "__main__"; on import it is the file's name.

quiz.q: What is the output of `list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, [1, 2, 3, 4]))`?
quiz.why: filter keeps only the items for which the lambda gives True: the even numbers 2 and 4.

quiz.q: `def add_item(item, lst=[])` is called twice: `add_item("a")`, then `add_item("b")`. What does the second call return?
quiz.why: The mutable default list is made only once and is shared between calls, so 'a' stayed. Fix: `lst=None`.

iq.q: What is a function and why do we use it?
iq.a: A function is a named, reusable block of code that takes input (parameters) and returns output. Benefits: no repeated code (DRY), easier testing, fix in one place and it is fixed everywhere, and a big program is split into small pieces that are easy to understand.

print only shows on the console and the function's result stays None. return gives the value back to the caller, which you can store in a variable and use further, and the function stops right at return. In production code functions return; print is only for debugging or CLI output.

iq.q: What are *args and **kwargs? When do you use them?
iq.a: *args takes a variable number of positional arguments into a tuple, **kwargs takes keyword arguments into a dict. Use: when the number of inputs isn't fixed, or when making a wrapper/decorator that passes arguments on: `def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return func(*args, **kwargs)`.

iq.q: Explain the mutable default argument problem.
iq.a: Default values are created only once, when the function is defined. In `def f(x, lst=[])` the same list is shared by every call, so data from earlier calls stays. Fix: use `lst=None` and inside write `if lst is None: lst = []`.

iq.q: What is lambda? What is its limitation?
iq.a: lambda is an anonymous one-line function: `lambda x: x * 2`. Mostly used for short logic in sort keys, map and filter. Limitation: only one expression, no statements (loop, assignment), and having no name makes debugging a bit harder. Use `def` for complex logic.

iq.q: Difference between map, filter and reduce?
iq.a: map applies a function to every item (output of the same length). filter keeps only the items where the function gives True. reduce (from functools) combines all items into one value, like a total: `reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums)`. In Python 3 map/filter give lazy iterators, so we wrap them in `list()`.

iq.q: What are local and global scope? The LEGB rule?
iq.a: A variable assigned inside a function is local and is visible only inside. One made at file level is global. Python looks for names in this order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. To change a global from inside use the `global` keyword; for the outer function's variable in a nested function use `nonlocal`.

iq.q: What is recursion? When is it better than iteration?
iq.a: A function calling itself with a smaller input and stopping at a base case. It feels natural for tree traversal, nested folders and divide-and-conquer (merge sort). Downside: every call uses stack memory and Python's limit is ~1000, so a loop is better for simple counting.

Every module has a `__name__`; if the file is run directly it is "__main__", if imported it is the module's name. Code inside this check runs only on a direct run. So one file can be both a reusable module and a standalone script, and test/training code doesn't run on its own when imported.

iq.q: Difference between a module and a package?
iq.a: A module is a single .py file. A package is a folder of modules (traditionally with `__init__.py`), like the `sklearn.linear_model` module inside the `sklearn` package. A library = a collection of packages installed with pip.

iq.q: In Python, are arguments pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
iq.a: Neither fully one nor the other: "pass by object reference". The function gets a reference to the object. If you modify a mutable object (list, dict) inside, it changes outside too; if you reassign an immutable one (int, str), only the local name changes and the outside one stays the same.

iq.q: What should the order of positional, keyword and default arguments be?
iq.a: In the definition: normal positional → *args → keyword-only/default → **kwargs, like `def f(a, b, *args, option=True, **kwargs)`. When calling, positional arguments come before keyword arguments; `f(a=1, 2)` is a SyntaxError.
